subject: radiology
title: Corkscrew Oesophagus, Achalasia and Oesophageal Signs

steps.title: Corkscrew from spasm
steps.tx: **Corkscrew oesophagus** twists the barium column into a helical, rosary like pattern during diffuse oesophageal spasm, when simultaneous non peristaltic contractions segment the tube instead of sweeping in sequence. The illustrated cutaway places that corkscrew beside reflux damage and hiatus hernia, the three oesophageal patterns examiners rotate. Between spasms the oesophagus can look completely normal, so a single quiet swallow never excludes the diagnosis.

steps.title: Spasm versus achalasia
steps.tx: **Diffuse spasm** keeps a working lower sphincter that relaxes on swallowing, so barium eventually empties and the oesophagus stays near normal calibre. Achalasia fails sphincter relaxation from lost myenteric neurons, dilating the oesophagus into a sigmoid reservoir ending in a smooth beak. Chest pain dominates spasm presentations, while regurgitation of undigested food and weight loss dominate achalasia, matching their opposite mechanics.

Chest pain dominates spasm, regurgitation dominates achalasia.

steps.title: Manometry settles motility
steps.tx: **High resolution manometry** measures pressure along the oesophagus during test swallows and classifies motility by the Chicago system. Achalasia shows a raised integrated relaxation pressure with absent peristalsis, split into subtypes by whether the body pressurises or spasms. Diffuse spasm instead shows premature rapid contractions with normal sphincter relaxation. Barium suggests the pattern, but manometry names it and steers dilation, myotomy or medical therapy.

steps.title: Schatzki ring and webs
steps.tx: **Schatzki ring** is a thin mucosal ring at the squamocolumnar junction that narrows the lumen only when it measures under about 13 mm, causing episodic solid food dysphagia called steakhouse syndrome. Oesophageal webs sit higher, thin shelves from the anterior wall of the cervical oesophagus, and pair with iron deficiency in Plummer Vinson syndrome. Both show best on a prone full column barium swallow distending the tube.

Oesophageal webs sit higher in the cervical oesophagus and pair with iron deficiency in Plummer Vinson syndrome. Both show best on a prone distended swallow.

steps.title: Feline oesophagus and eosinophils
steps.tx: **Feline oesophagus** draws fine transverse rings across the barium column from transient muscular folding, named after the cat oesophagus it resembles. Fixed concentric rings with longitudinal furrows and white exudates instead mark eosinophilic oesophagitis in a young atopic patient with food impactions. The barium study can look near normal in eosinophilic disease, so endoscopy with biopsies from several levels makes the diagnosis even through healthy looking mucosa.

steps.title: Candida and viral oesophagitis patterns
steps.tx: **Candida oesophagitis** coats barium with shaggy, plaque like filling defects giving a cobblestone or snakeskin wall in immunocompromised patients with odynophagia. Herpes simplex instead punches out multiple small discrete ulcers on normal mucosa, while cytomegalovirus cuts one or a few giant flat ulcers in advanced HIV. The barium pattern triages the organism, but endoscopic brushings and biopsies confirm before antifungal or antiviral therapy commits.

steps.title: Extrinsic impressions on the oesophagus
steps.tx: **Extrinsic compression** indents the barium column with smooth mucosa from structures crossing the oesophagus: an aberrant right subclavian artery slanting behind it causes dysphagia lusoria, and an enlarged left atrium pushes its anterior wall. The impression moves with the compressing structure and the mucosa stays intact, separating it from a submucosal tumour like leiomyoma, which makes a smooth obtuse defect inside the wall itself.

steps.title: Zenker diverticulum points backward
steps.tx: **Zenker diverticulum** pouches posteriorly through Killian dehiscence between the thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus muscles, just above the upper sphincter. Barium fills the sac behind the cervical oesophagus, and retained food inside it explains halitosis, regurgitation and aspiration in older patients. Endoscopy risks perforating the sac, so the barium study comes first and maps the neck of the pouch for the surgeon or stapling team.
